I’ve been thinking about KFF’s recent analysis of CMS-0057-F and the annual metrics that health plans are now required to post publicly, including approval and denial rates and decision turnaround times. 

That transparency is real progress. But visibility into the prior authorization (PA) process isn’t the same as improving it, and aggregate data points can’t tell us the whole story. There’s a bigger opportunity to understand where PA continues to break down and use that data to improve how plans operate.

UnitedHealthcare (UHC) will eliminate prior authorization requirements for approximately 1,700 procedure codes beginning October 1, advancing its goal of reducing authorization volume by 30% by year-end. 

The changes affect outpatient procedures including colonoscopies, endoscopies, arthroscopies, joint injections, hernia repairs, lesion excisions, fracture care, and selected genetic testing. 

UHC is also expanding exemptions for rural hospitals and pediatric specialties while moving more than 70% of prior authorizations to standardized electronic formats. 

Mejong Ayeb, Vice President for Revenue Cycle Market Operations at Providence, highlighted the difficulty of automation when payer policies frequently change. 

The American Medical Association (AMA) reports physicians average 40 prior authorizations weekly, while revenue cycle leaders remain concerned about retrospective audits, downcoding, medical necessity reviews, and documentation requirements.

Prior Authorization: What does it actually mean? 🤔

If your doctor says a service needs prior authorization, it doesn’t necessarily mean your care has been denied. It simply means your insurance wants to review and approve the service before agreeing to pay for it.

But how that process works can look very different depending on your Medicare coverage. Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage have different rules when it comes to prior authorization.

A little clarity can go a long way when navigating your Medicare coverage.  Learn more below!👇
